newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Millions of Moroccans vote on new parliament.
newsitem.headline: Millions of Moroccans vote on new parliament.

text.p: Millions of Moroccans voted on Friday in a referendum to change the constitution and set up a second house of parliament, moves seen as a way to decentralise power and help rural development.

King Hassan, pro-government and the main opposition parties had all called the people to vote in favour, and officials expect an overwhelming endorsement for a new second house with power to force a no-confidence vote in the government.

Provisional figures showed that one hour before the booths closed at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT) around 80 percent of the more than 12 million Moroccans eligible to vote had done so, an Interior Ministry official said.
"I voted today to respond to King Hassan's appeal," said Khadija al-Idrissi, a 42-year-old housewife, casting her ballot at the Lycee Hassan II in the capital, Rabat.

King Hassan, whose paramount powers will not be touched, says the changes with strengthen regional representation and will split the present 333-seat Majlis Anuwab (Chamber of Representatives) in two.

Officials see indirect elections to the new second house, mainly through local councils, professional bodies and trade unions, as a means of spreading political influence to areas of the country which have had little say in political decisions.

The proposed changes to the 1992 constitution are also widely seen as a way to help development in rural areas, home to 50 percent of the country's 27 million people, and a major contributor through farm products to foreign currency earnings.
At Moulay Youssef school, near the royal palace in Rabat, one young woman, casting ballots for herself and her husband, said: "I voted 'yes' because this is what my head told me."
In Casablanca, the main financial city, eyewitnesses reported a steady stream of voters, mainly women casting their ballots as they did their morning shopping.
Rachida Achak, a teacher voting in the city said: "I voted 'yes' because we are expecting our life to improve".
The king cast his vote in Skhirat, 20 kms (12 miles) from Rabat, at 3 p.m. (1500 GMT). Wearing a white blazer and green trousers, he waved and smiled to a cheering crowd.
White banners bearing the legend in Arabic "Referendum, 13 September" fluttered in sunshine outside booths as they opened in Rabat.
Among those eligible to vote are more than 118,000 people in the disputed Western Sahara.

"It's an historic moment for this country. For the first time there is a general consensus, including the opposition, to vote 'Yes' for the proposals," said one senior official on the eve of the vote.

The newly-created lower house, formed when the present parliament is split, will be directly elected, a demand long made by opposition parties. The current parliament has one-third of its members elected indirectly.

Morocco's main opposition parties, the old-guard Istiqlal party and Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP) have both called for a "Yes" vote, with only some small parties calling for a boycott or a 'No' vote.

One of the small parties, the Avant-Garde Democratic and Socialist Party, said on Friday that police had arrested 10 of its members while they were campaigning on Thursday for a boycott of the referendum. An Interior Ministry official said he was not aware of the arrests.
First results are expected late on Friday and a final tally on Saturday.
